newsitem.title: UK: British money supply shows economy blossoming.
newsitem.headline: British money supply shows economy blossoming.

text.p: Britain's money supply growth shot up in the year to August and consumer credit continued to increase, the Bank of England said on Thursday, indicating the economy is steaming ahead.
Economists said the sharp to 9.4 percent pick-up in broad money (M4) growth, above the government's three-to-nine percent monitoring range, suggested interest rates should head up, not down.

Figures from the British Bankers' Association showed consumer credit rose by 453 million pounds ($706.1 million) in August, down from July's 556 million increase but well above the recent monthly average of 405 million.
"All the data now are pointing to very firm economic recovery," said Jonathan Griggs, economist at Barclays Bank.

"The UK will look like one of the strongest economies in the world as we go into the pre-election countdown and I think the bias in interest rate markets has to increasingly shift towards...a pre-emptive hike."

Thursday's figures came just a day after August retail sales were shown to have leapt 1.0 percent, taking the three-month rate of growth to its strongest level in eight years and reviving memories of the late 1980s boom.

Griggs supported the line taken by Bank of England Governor Eddie George. Minutes of the July 30 meeting with Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke showed George wished to see official interest rates at 6.00 percent, not 5.75.
In those minutes George said money supply growth, often seen as a harbinger of future inflationary pressure, was consistent with rising demand growth this year and next.

The UK Treasury said the growth in August M4 was in part due to special factors, particularly the takeover of the National & Provincial building society by British bank Abbey National and subsequent payouts made to N&P account holders.
But economists said the N&P takeover was offset by a fall in gilt repos included in M4.

They said the bounce in M4 growth, after it's tumble to 9.0 percent in July, merely confirmed what most UK data have been singing from the rooftops -- Britain's economy is growing fast as consumers queue up to spend.
